explanation:
[EFFECT] Higher wind speed consistently reduces the model's predicted bike demand — the effect is broadly monotonically decreasing. At very low wind speeds (near calm, roughly 0–7 km/h), the contribution is close to zero or very slightly positive. As wind picks up beyond about 20 km/h (normalised value ~0.30), the contribution turns meaningfully negative, and at the highest observed speeds (~40–57 km/h, normalised ~0.60–0.85) the penalty on predicted demand becomes quite severe, with SHAP values reaching –0.4 to –0.7 in log space. There is no reversal — wind never helps demand; it only hurts it, more so as it gets stronger.

[IMPORTANCE] Windspeed is the **second-least important** feature in the model, ranking **8th out of 9** with an importance score of about 0.020. This is roughly 40 times smaller than the top feature (hour of day) and about one-quarter the influence of humidity, the next feature above it. In practice, windspeed has a real but limited overall influence on predicted rentals compared to time-of-day, temperature, or season.

[RECOMMENDATION] When high wind speeds are forecast (above roughly 20 km/h), planners can reasonably expect somewhat softer demand and may consider reducing the number of bikes deployed or staff scheduled for those hours, saving resources without significantly under-serving customers.
